cap-L1#0.why: When a battery connects to the plates, it pushes electrons onto one plate and pulls them off the other. The plates now hold opposite charges. They attract each other across the gap, but the insulator will not let electrons cross. So the charges just sit there, pulling on each other. That pull is an electric field in the gap, and the field holds the stored energy. If the gap were a conductor, the charge would flow across and nothing would be stored.
cap-L1#0.pic: Draw two parallel horizontal lines for the plates. Put plus signs along the top one and minus signs along the bottom one. Draw short arrows in the gap pointing from the top plate down to the bottom plate. Those arrows are the field.
cap-L1#0.analogy: Think of a stretched rubber band held between two fingers. The stretch is the stored energy. The plates are your fingers, the charge difference is the stretch, and the field is the tension. It breaks down because a rubber band stretches for any size, but a real capacitor has a voltage limit where the insulator fails.
ways: Charge separated by an insulator stores energy in the gap, not in the metal.
Connect a 9 V battery, then remove it. The plates keep their opposite charge and still show 9 V on a meter.
Capacitor = tiny short-term energy tank. A battery = big long-term energy tank.

ex.q: A 100 uF capacitor is charged to 9 V. How much energy is in its field?
steps: Use the energy formula E = 1/2 C V^2 because the energy is in the field.

cap-L1#0.trap: Thinking the energy sits inside the metal plates. It sits in the electric field in the insulating gap.
cap-L1#0.tip: Plates plus a gap: charge can't hop, so it waits and pulls.

cap-L1#1.why: Capacitance tells how easily a capacitor takes in charge for each volt pushed on it. Bigger plates have more room for charge. Plates closer together pull harder on each other, so more charge fits at the same voltage. The ratio Q/V stays the same for a given capacitor, so it is a fixed property, like the size of a bucket. A farad is huge, which is why real parts use microfarads (uF).
cap-L1#1.pic: Draw a bucket. The width of the bucket is the capacitance C. The water level is the voltage V. The amount of water is the charge Q. Mark the level with a line and shade the water below it.
cap-L1#1.analogy: A wide bucket versus a narrow bucket: at the same water level, the wide one holds more water. Bucket width is C, water level is V, water volume is Q. It stops working because a bucket can be any shape, while capacitance is fixed by plate area and gap only.
ways: Capacitance is charge stored per volt.
C = 10 uF. At 2 V: Q = 20 uC. At 4 V: Q = 40 uC. Q doubles when V doubles.
Plot Q (up) against V (across). It is a straight line through zero. The slope is C.

ex.q: A capacitor holds 30 uC of charge at 6 V. What is C?
steps: Pick the formula C = Q / V.
Write Q = 30 uC and V = 6 V.
Units: uC per volt is uF.

cap-L1#1.trap: Mixing units. uF and uC are millionths. Keep the prefix on both and the answer stays clean.
cap-L1#1.tip: Farad = bucket size. Charge per volt.

cap-L1#2.why: The voltage squared appears because there are two things growing at once. To add more charge you must push against the charge already there. Double the voltage means double the charge on the plates, and each bit of charge is pushed in at double the voltage. Two doubles make a quadruple. So energy rises with the square of V. That is why a small voltage rise can make a capacitor much more dangerous.
cap-L1#2.pic: Draw a graph of V (up) against Q (across). It is a straight line from the origin. Shade the triangle under the line. The area of that triangle, 1/2 x Q x V, is the stored energy.
cap-L1#2.analogy: Compressing a spring: the more it is squeezed, the harder you must push, so the second half costs more than the first. Squeeze is the charge, push is the voltage. It stops working because a spring has a break point set by metal, but a capacitor limit is set by the insulator.
ways: Half the voltage gives one fourth of the energy.
C = 10 uF. 5 V gives 125 uJ. 10 V gives 500 uJ. Twice the volts, four times the energy.
Change V by a factor of k and energy changes by k^2.

ex.q: Voltage across a 20 uF capacitor goes from 5 V to 15 V. How many times bigger is the energy?
steps: Energy depends on V^2, so compare squares.
At 15 V E = 2250 uJ, which is 9 times 250 uJ.

cap-L1#2.trap: Saying double voltage gives double energy. Square it: double gives four times.

cap-L2#0.why: Parallel capacitors act like one bigger set of plates, so their areas add and capacitance adds. In series, the charge on each one must be the same, and the voltage splits between them. The total gap the voltage must cross is longer, so less charge fits per volt. That is why series gives a smaller total, the opposite of resistors. Series total is always less than the smallest one.
cap-L2#0.pic: Draw two capacitors side by side between the same two wires for parallel. Then draw them end to end on one wire for series. Label parallel Plates add. Label series Gaps add.
cap-L2#0.analogy: Parallel is like two buckets filling from the same tap: the total space adds. Series is like a bucket with a second bucket stacked below it, sharing the same stream. It stops working because the series stack is about voltage sharing, which water does not show well.
ways: Parallel: add. Series: reciprocal rule, like parallel resistors.
4 uF and 12 uF. Parallel: 16 uF. Series: (4 x 12)/(4 + 12) = 3 uF.
Capacitors do the opposite of resistors. Parallel adds, series shrinks.

ex.q: Find the series capacitance of 6 uF and 3 uF.
steps: Two capacitors, so product over sum works.
18 / 9 = 2 uF, smaller than 3 uF, which makes sense.

cap-L2#0.trap: Using the resistor rules by habit. Capacitors flip them: parallel adds.
cap-L2#0.tip: Caps are the mirror of resistors.

cap-L2#1.why: A capacitor charges until its voltage equals the supply. Once they match, nothing pushes more charge on. The current drops to zero. The insulator in the gap blocks any steady flow, so for steady DC it looks like a broken wire. During charging, current flows briefly. After that, it is quiet. If the capacitor still passed steady current, the plates could not hold a charge.
cap-L2#1.pic: Draw a circuit with a battery, a resistor, and a capacitor in a loop. Draw an arrow on the wire labeled big at the start. Then draw the same arrow crossed out later with the label zero.
cap-L2#1.analogy: A balloon being blown up through a pipe: at first air rushes in, then the balloon is full and the air stops. Air flow is current, balloon pressure is capacitor voltage. It stops working because a balloon can pop slowly and leak, while a good capacitor holds its charge.
ways: Full capacitor: no more current, so treat it as open.
9 V battery, 1 kilohm resistor, capacitor. Start: 9 mA. Later: 0 mA, and the capacitor reads 9 V.
Plot current against time: it starts high and falls to zero. Plot capacitor voltage: it starts at zero and rises to 9 V.

ex.q: A 12 V battery, a 2 kilohm resistor, and a capacitor are in series. After a long time, what is the current and the capacitor voltage?
steps: A full capacitor blocks steady current, so I = 0.
With I = 0, the resistor drops V = I x R = 0.
All 12 V must be across the capacitor.

cap-L2#1.trap: Saying the capacitor has no voltage when current stops. Zero current means full voltage.
cap-L2#1.tip: Full cap, closed gap? No: full cap, open gap.

circ-L1#0.why: In a series circuit the wire has no branches, so every charge must pass through every part, one after another. Charge cannot pile up or vanish, so the current is the same at each point. Each resistor adds more squeeze on the same path, so the resistances add up. If one part breaks, the one path is cut and nothing can flow anywhere. That is why old holiday lights went dark all at once when one bulb failed.
circ-L1#0.pic: Draw a single loop: battery, then three boxes (resistors) in a row, then back to the battery. Write the same arrow and the letter I beside each box. Put a small break in the loop and cross out the arrows to show nothing flows.
circ-L1#0.analogy: A single-lane road with three toll booths. Every car must go through all three booths, and the traffic rate is the same everywhere. Cars = charge, booths = resistors, cars per minute = current. It stops working because toll booths do not use up cars, while resistors do not use up charge either, but they do use up voltage.
ways: One path. Same current. Resistances add. One break stops all.
100 ohm + 220 ohm + 330 ohm = 650 ohm. On 13 V the current is 13 / 650 = 0.02 A everywhere.
Series: current same, resistance adds, voltage shares.

ex.q: Resistors of 100, 220 and 330 ohms are in series with a 13 V battery. Find the current.
steps: That makes 650 ohms total, because each adds squeeze.
Use I = V / R since the battery sets the total push.
The current is the same in all three resistors.

circ-L1#0.trap: Students think the current gets used up after each resistor. It does not. Voltage gets used up, current stays the same. Also, a broken part in series stops everything.
circ-L1#0.tip: Series = single file. One line, one current.

circ-L1#1.why: In parallel, the battery connects straight across every branch, so every branch gets the full voltage. Each branch pulls its own current, and the currents add up at the junction. Adding another branch gives the charge one more road, so the total current goes up. More current from the same voltage means smaller total resistance. That is why the total is always smaller than the smallest branch.
circ-L1#1.pic: Draw a ladder lying on its side: a battery on the left and two or three rungs (resistors) between the top and bottom rails. Mark each rung with the same voltage V. Draw arrows splitting at the top and merging at the bottom.
circ-L1#1.analogy: A store with several checkout lanes open. Each lane can serve customers at the same time, so the total customers per minute rises when you open one more. Lanes = branches, customers per minute = current. It stops working because customers choose lanes freely, but current always favors the lower-resistance branch.
ways: Many paths. Same voltage. Currents add. Total resistance drops.
12 ohm, 6 ohm, 4 ohm in parallel: 1/12 + 2/12 + 3/12 = 6/12, so R = 2 ohm. That is below 4.
Parallel total is always smaller than the smallest branch.

ex.q: Resistors of 12, 6 and 4 ohms are in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance.
steps: Write with a common bottom of 12: 1/12 + 2/12 + 3/12.
Check: 2 is smaller than the smallest branch (4). Good.

circ-L1#1.trap: Forgetting to flip at the end. 1/R = 1/2 is not R = 1/2 in this case: the answer is R = 2. Always check that your answer is smaller than the smallest branch.

circ-L1#2.why: The product-over-sum shortcut comes from the reciprocal rule. Start with 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. Put the two fractions over a common bottom: (R2 + R1) / (R1 x R2). Flip both sides and you get R = (R1 x R2) / (R1 + R2). The shortcut only works for exactly two resistors. If one resistor is far bigger than the other, the answer is close to the smaller one, because most current takes the easy path.
circ-L1#2.pic: Draw two resistors in parallel and label them R1 and R2. Beside it, draw one resistor labeled with the product over the sum as a fraction. Draw a number line and mark R1, R2, and the answer sitting to the left of both.
circ-L1#2.analogy: Two doors out of a gym: a wide door and a narrow door. Most students leave through the wide door, so the total exit speed is a bit more than the wide door alone. Doors = resistors (a wide door is a small resistance). It stops working because doors are not about voltage, but the way the easy path wins is the same.
ways: Multiply the two, divide by their sum.
The answer is always a bit smaller than the smaller resistor.

ex.q: A 40 ohm and a 60 ohm resistor are in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance.
steps: Only two resistors, so product over sum works.
Check: 24 is below 40, the smaller one. Good.

circ-L1#2.trap: Using product over sum for three or more resistors. It only works for two at a time. Also, do not add the resistors in the bottom only; the bottom is the sum, the top is the product.
circ-L1#2.tip: Parallel pair: product over sum, the shortcut for just two.

circ-L2#0.why: If all n resistors are the same size R, each branch takes the same current. The total current is n times one branch current, with the same voltage. So the total resistance is the voltage divided by n times the branch current, which is R divided by n. Think of it as n identical doors: n times the flow means 1/n of the squeeze. It is a fast shortcut you can check in your head.
circ-L2#0.pic: Draw three identical boxes in parallel, each labeled 90 ohm. Next to it draw one box labeled 30 ohm. Between them write an equals sign and the words divide by 3.
circ-L2#0.analogy: Three identical straws in one drink. Drinking through three straws is three times easier than one, so the squeeze is one third. Straws = resistors, ease of drinking = current. It stops working because with straws the sip depends on lungs, but a battery holds a fixed voltage.
ways: n equal resistors in parallel give R divided by n.
Two 100 ohm: 50. Four 100 ohm: 25. Ten 100 ohm: 10.
Plot R/n against n. It curves down quickly: big drop from 1 to 2, smaller drops after.

ex.q: Four 200 ohm resistors are in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
steps: All four are equal, so use R / n.
Check: 50 is less than 200, as parallel should be.
This beats the long reciprocal sum and is easy to do mentally.

circ-L2#0.trap: Using it when the resistors are different sizes. The shortcut only works for identical resistors. Also do not multiply by n; that would be series.
circ-L2#0.tip: n twins side by side: divide by n.

circ-L2#1.why: A short is a path with almost zero resistance. In parallel it gets the same voltage as everything else. By Ohm's law, current is V / R, and with R near zero the current is huge. Nearly all the current takes that easy path, so the other parts get almost nothing and go dark. The huge current heats the wires and the source. That is why shorts cause fires and why fuses exist.
circ-L2#1.pic: Draw a battery, a lamp, and a plain wire jumping across the lamp from top to bottom. Draw a thick arrow through the wire and a tiny thin arrow through the lamp. Write the lamp voltage as about 0 V.
circ-L2#1.analogy: A river with a small side channel and a huge waterfall shortcut next to it. Almost all the water takes the shortcut and the mill wheel on the side channel stops. Water = current, mill wheel = the lamp. It stops working because water has no source limit, while a real battery can overheat and be damaged.
ways: A wire across a part gives current a free road. The part gets nothing.
9 V, a 10 ohm resistor, and a 0.1 ohm wire in parallel. Resistor current 0.9 A. Wire current 9 / 0.1 = 90 A. The wire takes 99 percent.
Current always picks the path with the least resistance.

ex.q: A 9 V source has a 10 ohm lamp and a 0.1 ohm wire in parallel. How much current flows in the wire? (Ignore the source resistance.)
steps: Parallel branches all get the full 9 V.
Use I = V / R for the wire branch.
Compare: the lamp only gets 9 / 10 = 0.9 A.
Answer: 90 A in the wire, 100 times more than the lamp.

circ-L2#1.trap: Students think a short makes the circuit have no current. It does the opposite: a short gives a huge current. The part you shorted goes dark, but the source is in danger.
circ-L2#1.tip: Short = shortcut, and all the traffic takes it.

circ-L2#2.why: A mixed circuit has both series and parallel pieces, so no single rule fits it all. The trick is to shrink it. Find a spot that is clearly parallel or clearly series, replace it with its one equivalent resistor, and redraw. Each step makes the picture simpler without changing what the battery sees. Repeat until one resistor is left. Always work from the inside out, parallel groups first when they sit in a series path.
circ-L2#2.pic: Draw the original circuit. Circle the parallel group with a pencil. Then draw a second picture with that group replaced by one box. Keep going until you have a single box next to the battery.
circ-L2#2.analogy: Packing a suitcase inside a bigger suitcase. You pack small bags first, then put those inside bigger ones. Small bags = parallel groups, bigger bag = series path. It stops working because suitcases have size limits, while circuits do not.
ways: Replace each parallel group by one resistor, then add the series parts.
10 ohm in series with two 20 ohm in parallel. 20 || 20 = 10. Then 10 + 10 = 20 ohm.
Parallel first, then series, redraw each time.

ex.q: A 12 ohm resistor is in series with a parallel pair of 30 ohm and 60 ohm. Find the total resistance.
steps: Redraw: the pair becomes one 20 ohm resistor.
Now 12 and 20 are in series, so they add.

circ-L2#2.trap: Adding everything together without noticing the parallel part. Always ask: is this pair side by side (parallel) or end to end (series)?
circ-L2#2.tip: Shrink it, redraw it, repeat it.

circ-L3#0.why: In series, the same current goes through every resistor. Ohm's law then says V = I x R, so a bigger resistor gets a bigger voltage drop. The total drop must equal the battery voltage. So each resistor takes its fraction of the supply, equal to its share of the total resistance. This is the voltage divider. It is how you make a smaller voltage out of a bigger one.
circ-L3#0.pic: Draw a battery on top, with two stacked resistors in a column and ground at the bottom. Mark the junction in the middle. Write V2 beside the bottom resistor and draw its share as a part of the total height.
circ-L3#0.analogy: Sharing a pizza by how hungry each person is. A bigger resistor eats a bigger slice of the battery voltage. Pizza = voltage, hunger = resistance. It stops working because pizza slices are food, but voltage does not run out in the wire; it only drops across parts.
ways: Each resistor gets a voltage in proportion to its resistance.
9 V, 2 k and 6 k. Total 8 k. Share of R2 = 6/8. V2 = 6.75 V. V1 = 2.25 V. They add to 9 V.
The bigger resistor gets the bigger share of voltage.

ex.q: A 15 V source feeds R1 = 4 k in series with R2 = 6 k. Find the voltage across R2.
steps: Same current goes through both, so voltage splits by resistance.
Answer: 9 V (and R1 gets 6 V, adding to 15).

circ-L3#0.trap: Putting the wrong resistor on top. The numerator is the resistor you want the voltage across. Check that the two drops add to the supply.
circ-L3#0.tip: Big resistor, big slice of the voltage.

circ-L3#1.why: In parallel, both branches have the same voltage, so each current is V / R. The smaller resistor lets more current flow. The total current is the sum of the two. Taking each branch's share gives I1 = I x R2 / (R1 + R2). Notice the other resistor is on top: the branch with less resistance gets the bigger share, so its fraction has the larger number on top.
circ-L3#1.pic: Draw a wire splitting into two branches. Make the branch with the smaller resistor thicker and the branch with the bigger resistor thinner. Write the currents next to each. Show that they merge again below.
circ-L3#1.analogy: A crowd leaving a stadium through a wide gate and a narrow gate. More people use the wide gate. Wide gate = small resistance, people = current. It stops working because people choose, while current splits exactly by the math.
ways: Current splits unevenly. The smaller resistor takes the larger share.
12 A into 6 ohm and 3 ohm. R1 gets 12 x 3/9 = 4 A. R2 gets 12 x 6/9 = 8 A. They add to 12 A.
Current goes to the easy path.

ex.q: 20 A splits between R1 = 4 ohm and R2 = 12 ohm in parallel. Find the current in R1.
steps: Both branches share the same voltage, so smaller R gets more current.
Formula: I1 = I x R2 / (R1 + R2).
Check R2: 20 - 15 = 5 A. The 12 ohm gets less, as it should.

circ-L3#1.trap: Using R1 on top instead of R2, which gives the answer swapped. The smaller resistor must get the bigger current, so check the answer makes sense.
circ-L3#1.tip: Cross over: the other resistor goes on top.

circ-L3#2.why: Brightness depends on power. In series, current is the same through each bulb, so P = I^2 x R and the bulb with the biggest resistance gets the most power. In parallel, voltage is the same across each bulb, so P = V^2 / R and the bulb with the smallest resistance gets the most power. Each parallel bulb has its own path, so removing one does not stop the others. In series, removing one breaks the only path.
circ-L3#2.pic: Draw two bulbs in series, then two bulbs in parallel. Under the series picture write I the same and P = I^2 R. Under the parallel picture write V the same and P = V^2 / R. Make the brighter bulb bigger in each picture.
circ-L3#2.analogy: A relay race versus a group of runners racing side by side. In the relay (series) everyone runs the same number of steps, the one with the heaviest load works hardest. In side by side (parallel) each runner has the same track. Heaviest load = biggest R. It stops working because runners get tired but bulbs do not.
ways: Series: biggest R is brightest. Parallel: smallest R is brightest.
Series, 10 V, bulbs 2 ohm and 8 ohm: I = 1 A, P = 2 W and 8 W. Parallel, 12 V: P = 144/2 = 72 W and 144/8 = 18 W.
Same current: use I^2R. Same voltage: use V^2/R.

ex.q: Bulbs of 2 ohm and 8 ohm are in series across 10 V. Which is brighter, and what is each power?
steps: Current: 10 / 10 = 1 A, the same in both.
Same current, so use P = I^2 x R.
2 ohm bulb: 1 x 1 x 2 = 2 W. 8 ohm bulb: 1 x 1 x 8 = 8 W.
The 8 ohm bulb has more power.
Answer: the 8 ohm bulb is brighter, 8 W versus 2 W.

circ-L3#2.trap: Using the wrong power formula. In series the current is shared, so use I^2 R. In parallel the voltage is shared, so use V^2 / R. The winner flips.
circ-L3#2.tip: Series: big R shines. Parallel: small R shines.

circ-L4#0.why: An open circuit is a break. No charge can cross the gap, so the current is zero everywhere in that series loop. With zero current, the other parts have zero voltage drop (V = I x R = 0), so the whole battery voltage appears across the break. A short is the opposite: a path with tiny resistance. Huge current flows, and that creates heat. Both are faults, but they look very different on a meter.
circ-L4#0.pic: Draw a loop with a battery, lamp, and a switch. Show the switch open with a gap. Write 0 V across the lamp and 9 V across the gap. Next to it draw the same loop with a thick wire across the lamp and write the words big current.
circ-L4#0.analogy: A drawbridge. When the bridge is up (open), no cars cross, and all the height difference shows up at the gap. When a tunnel is dug straight through (short), a flood of cars rushes through. Cars = current. It stops working because a bridge gap is not about pressure, but it matches the idea well.
ways: Open: current zero, voltage across the gap is the full battery. Short: current huge, voltage across it near zero.
9 V battery, 100 ohm lamp, switch open: I = 0, lamp 0 V, switch 9 V. Switch closed: I = 0.09 A, lamp 9 V, switch 0 V.
Open = all the voltage. Short = none of the voltage.

ex.q: A 6 V battery, a 50 ohm lamp, and a switch are in series. The switch is open. What is the voltage across the lamp and across the switch?
steps: Open switch means no path, so I = 0.
Lamp: V = I x R = 0 x 50 = 0 V.
The battery voltage must be dropped somewhere.
Kirchhoff: the drops add to 6 V, so the switch has it all.
Check by closing the switch: the lamp would get all 6 V.

circ-L4#0.trap: Believing that open means 0 V everywhere. The break itself has the full voltage. A meter across an open gap reads the battery voltage.
circ-L4#0.tip: Open gap, full voltage. Short wire, zero voltage.

circ-L4#1.why: A voltmeter must not change the circuit it measures, so it has huge resistance and is placed across the part (parallel). Almost no current goes through it. An ammeter must measure the same current that was flowing, so it goes in the path (series) and has tiny resistance. If you put an ammeter across a battery, you make a near short: huge current, a blown fuse, or a damaged meter. If you put a voltmeter in series, its huge resistance blocks nearly all current.
circ-L4#1.pic: Draw a loop with a battery and a lamp. Draw a circle with V across the lamp (two wires). Draw a second circle with A cut into the loop wire. Label V as parallel and A as series.
circ-L4#1.analogy: A water meter and a pressure gauge. The flow meter sits in the pipe (series) and counts water passing. The pressure gauge taps the pipe from the side (parallel) and barely uses any water. Flow meter = ammeter, pressure gauge = voltmeter. It stops working because real flow meters slow the water a bit, much as an ammeter adds a tiny resistance.
ways: Voltmeter: parallel, high resistance. Ammeter: series, tiny resistance.
Ammeter 0.1 ohm across 9 V: I = 90 A (bad). Voltmeter 1 Mohm across 9 V: I = 9 microamps (fine).
V is for Voltage, parallel. A is for Amps, series.

ex.q: An ammeter with 0.2 ohm resistance is accidentally connected directly across a 9 V battery. What current would flow (ignore the battery's own resistance)?
steps: The ammeter is in parallel with the battery, a near short.
That is far more than a meter's range or a fuse rating.
Answer: 45 A, which would blow the fuse or damage the meter.

circ-L4#1.trap: Mixing up where each meter goes. Voltmeters go across a part. Ammeters go in the line with the part. If you need to measure current, break the circuit and insert the meter.
circ-L4#1.tip: Volts in parallel, amps in series, never amps across a battery.

circ-L4#2.why: Power in the load is P = I^2 x R. If the load resistance is very small, the current is big but the load voltage is tiny, so power is small. If the load is very big, the voltage is big but the current is tiny, so power is small. Somewhere in the middle there is a peak, and it happens when the load resistance equals the source's own resistance. At that point half the power is lost in the source, so the efficiency is only 50 percent.
circ-L4#2.pic: Draw a graph with load resistance on the bottom and power up the side. The curve rises quickly, peaks, then falls slowly. Mark the peak where R load = R source.
circ-L4#2.analogy: Pushing a shopping cart: the best push comes when your effort matches the weight. Too light a load wastes the push and too heavy a load will not move. Effort = source, cart = load. It stops working because the cart does not have a clear peak the way power does.
ways: Maximum power goes to the load when load resistance equals source resistance.
12 V source with 4 ohm inside. Load 2 ohm: 8 W. Load 4 ohm: 9 W. Load 8 ohm: 8 W. The peak is at 4 ohm.
The curve peaks at R load = R source.

ex.q: A 12 V source has 4 ohm of internal resistance. Find the load power for a 4 ohm load.
steps: Load power: P = I^2 x R = 1.5 x 1.5 x 4.
That is the peak: 2 ohm and 8 ohm loads both give 8 W.

circ-L4#2.trap: Thinking max power also means max efficiency. At the peak, half of the power is wasted inside the source. Also, the card's check question is a simple voltage divider: 12 V across 1 k and 3 k gives 9 V on the 3 k.
circ-L4#2.tip: Match the load to the source to get the most watts.

circ-L4#3.why: Circuits obey conservation laws. Energy cannot appear from nowhere, so the power the source supplies must equal the power the resistors turn into heat. Charge cannot vanish, so currents entering a junction equal currents leaving. Energy per charge cannot go missing around a loop, so the rises and drops balance. If your answers break any of these, you made an arithmetic or setup error. These checks cost seconds and catch most mistakes.
circ-L4#3.pic: Draw a loop with a battery and three resistors. Write the voltage drop beside each resistor. Under it draw a small bar chart: one tall bar for the battery and three short bars stacked to the same height.
circ-L4#3.analogy: A bank account: money in must equal money out plus what remains. Battery = deposits, resistors = withdrawals. If the total does not balance, someone made a counting error. It stops working because a bank can run low, while a circuit always balances exactly.
ways: Check power in = power out, branch currents add, loop drops add up.
24 V battery. Drops 5 V and 3 V. Third = 24 - 5 - 3 = 16 V. Sum = 24 V. Balanced.
If it does not add up, something is wrong.

ex.q: A 24 V battery drives three series resistors. Two drop 5 V and 3 V. Find the third drop and check it.
steps: Kirchhoff: drops around the loop add to the battery voltage.
If the current were 2 A, the power would be 48 W from the source and 10 + 6 + 32 = 48 W in the resistors.

circ-L4#3.trap: Skipping the check. A quick sum catches mistakes like a lost minus sign or a wrong resistor. Add the drops every time.
circ-L4#3.tip: What goes in must come out: check your sums.

ctrl-L1#0.why: A switch has poles and throws. A pole is one moving contact that carries one circuit. A throw is a position the pole can connect to. The letters in the name count these. Counting terminals is simple: each pole has one common terminal plus one terminal per throw. That is why the four types differ in how many wires they hold and what they can do.
ctrl-L1#0.pic: Draw a small box for each type. For SPST draw one lever and one contact. For SPDT draw one lever with two contacts, top and bottom. For DPST draw two SPST levers joined by a dotted line. For DPDT draw two SPDT levers joined by a dotted line.
ctrl-L1#0.analogy: A traffic cop at an intersection. One cop (pole) can point cars down one road (SPST) or choose between two roads (SPDT). Two cops moving together are DPST or DPDT. Cop = pole, road = throw. It stops working because cops are not electrically separate, but poles are.
ways: S = single, D = double. P = pole, T = throw. So SPDT is single pole, double throw.
Terminals = poles x (throws + 1). SPST 2. SPDT 3. DPST 4. DPDT 6.
Double pole means two circuits at once. Double throw means two choices.

ex.q: How many terminals does a DPDT switch have, and why?
steps: DPDT means double pole, double throw.
Each pole has one common terminal plus two throw terminals.

ctrl-L1#0.trap: Confusing poles with throws. Pole = how many circuits you control. Throw = how many positions each one can connect. Do not just count the letters.

ctrl-L1#1.why: Pole and throw describe two different jobs. A pole is a circuit the switch controls, so more poles means more circuits switched at once. A throw is a choice of position, so more throws means more places to send current. SPDT sends one circuit to one of two places. Because the name says what it does, you can read it like a label. S or D at the front is the pole count, and S or D at the end is the throw count.
ctrl-L1#1.pic: Draw an SPDT switch: a pivot on the left, a lever, and two contacts on the right (top and bottom). Label the pivot as the pole. Label the two contacts as the throws. Draw an arrow showing the lever flipping between them.
ctrl-L1#1.analogy: A TV remote with a switch for inputs: one remote (single pole) picks between HDMI 1 and HDMI 2 (double throw). Pole = remote, throw = input choice. It stops working because the remote has no wires, but the idea of one controller with two choices is correct.
ways: Pole = circuits controlled. Throw = positions per circuit.
SPDT: 1 pole, 2 throws, 3 terminals. DPST: 2 poles, 1 throw, 4 terminals.
One lever on the left, two contacts on the right is SPDT.

ex.q: An SPDT switch is built into a headphone box to choose speaker A or speaker B. How many poles and throws, and can both speakers play at once?
steps: One pole means one circuit (the audio signal) is switched.
Two throws mean the lever picks speaker A or speaker B.
The lever can touch only one contact at a time.
So only one speaker plays at a time.
Answer: 1 pole, 2 throws, only one speaker at once.

ctrl-L1#1.trap: Reading the letters wrong. The first letter is the number of poles, the last letter is the number of throws. SPDT is not 'single position, double...'.
ctrl-L1#1.tip: First letter counts circuits, last letter counts choices.

ctrl-L1#2.why: A fuse is a thin wire made to be the weakest link. Current heats it by P = I^2 x R. Normal current makes only a little heat, so it stays whole. Too much current makes much more heat, because heat grows with the square of the current. The wire melts and opens the circuit. It must be in series so all the load current has to pass through it. A fuse that blows is telling you there is a fault, so fix it first or the new fuse blows too.
ctrl-L1#2.pic: Draw a battery, a fuse (a small glass tube with a curvy wire inside), and a lamp in one loop. Beside it draw the fuse with the thin wire melted and a gap, and put an X on the loop.
ctrl-L1#2.analogy: A fuse is like a sacrificial bodyguard. It takes the hit so the expensive stuff survives. Fuse = bodyguard, damage = overcurrent. It stops working because a bodyguard can fight back, while a fuse is used up.
ways: Thin wire. Too much current melts it. One use. Series with the load.
Fuse wire 0.05 ohm. At 10 A: 5 W of heat. At 20 A: 20 W of heat. Double current means four times the heat.
Fuse protects wires and devices, in series, fix first.

ex.q: A 0.05 ohm fuse wire carries 10 A normally. A fault pushes the current to 30 A. How much does the heating change?
steps: Heat power is P = I^2 x R.
Tripling the current gave nine times the heat (3 squared).
Answer: 45 W, nine times the normal heat, so the fuse melts.

ctrl-L1#2.trap: Putting the fuse in parallel with the load. In parallel it would not carry the load current and would not protect anything (and it would short the source). Always place it in series.
ctrl-L1#2.tip: Fuse in series, fix the fault, then replace.

ctrl-L2#0.why: A breaker does the same job as a fuse, but it can be reset. Inside, a strip of two metals bends when it heats up, or a magnet pulls a latch when the current is very large. Either way the switch flips open. After you remove the cause and let it cool, you flip it back. It is slower than a fuse for small overloads because heating the strip takes time. The slow part is on purpose so that brief start-up surges do not trip it.
ctrl-L2#0.pic: Draw a switch in a box with a bent strip of two colors above it. Draw heat arrows near the strip and show the strip bending upward to push the switch open. Add a handle that you can flip back.
ctrl-L2#0.analogy: A circuit breaker is like a pop-up toaster handle: it springs up when it gets too hot, and you push it down to restart. Handle = switch, heat = overload. It stops working because a toaster pops by timer, but a breaker pops by current.
ways: Trips on too much current. Reset by hand. Fix the cause first.
A 15 A breaker on 120 V allows 1800 W. A 1500 W heater plus a 600 W dryer is 2100 W, which is 17.5 A, so it trips.

ex.q: A 15 A breaker is on a 120 V circuit. A 1500 W heater and a 600 W hair dryer run together. Will it trip?
steps: Current from P = V x I, so I = P / V.

ctrl-L2#0.trap: Resetting it again and again without fixing the problem. A trip means too much current. Unplug something first, then reset.
ctrl-L2#0.tip: Breaker: bend, flip, reset after you fix.

ctrl-L2#1.why: A fuse must be bigger than the normal current, or it would blow every time. But it must be small enough to protect the wire. So find the normal current first with I = P / V, then pick the next standard size above it. The gap lets small surges through without blowing, yet a real fault goes well past the rating. Picking a much bigger fuse is dangerous, because the wire could overheat before the fuse reacts.
ctrl-L2#1.pic: Draw a number line with the standard fuse sizes 5, 10, 15, 20 marked as tick marks. Plot the calculated current as a dot between two ticks. Draw an arrow from the dot to the next tick above.
ctrl-L2#1.analogy: Buying a jacket: you pick the next size up from your measurement so it fits. Your measurement = calculated current, jacket sizes = standard fuses. It stops working because a jacket that is too big is only baggy, while a fuse that is too big can be unsafe.
ways: Find I = P / V, then use the next larger standard fuse.
1500 W at 120 V is 12.5 A. Standard fuses: 5, 10, 15, 20. Pick 15 A.
Round up to the next fuse, not a way-bigger one.

ex.q: A 1500 W toaster oven runs on 120 V. Choose the smallest fuse from 5, 10, 15, 20 A that will not blow in normal use.
steps: Use P = V x I, so I = P / V.
A 10 A fuse is too small and would blow.
The next standard size above 12.5 A is 15 A.

ctrl-L2#1.trap: Choosing a fuse that is just below the current (it would blow) or far above it (it would not protect). Always go to the next standard value above the calculated current.
ctrl-L2#1.tip: Find the amps, then step up one size.

ctrl-L2#2.why: Current should leave through the hot wire and come back through the neutral wire, in equal amounts. If some current leaks out another way, like through a person to the ground, the return is smaller. A GFCI compares the two currents all the time. If they differ by about 5 mA, it trips in milliseconds. A fuse or breaker would not notice 5 mA, since it only reacts to many amps. So the GFCI protects people, while breakers protect the wires.
ctrl-L2#2.pic: Draw a wall outlet with two wires going to a device: hot out and neutral back. Put a small box in the middle labeled GFCI that compares the two arrows. Then draw a leak path from the device through a stick figure to the ground.
ctrl-L2#2.analogy: A lifeguard counting swimmers: the number who go into the pool must equal the number who come out. If one is missing, an alarm goes off. Swimmers = current, lifeguard = GFCI. It stops working because swimmers are separate people, but current is measured as a tiny difference.
ways: If outgoing and returning current differ by about 5 mA, trip fast.
Hot carries 10.000 A out. Neutral returns 9.990 A. The 0.010 A (10 mA) leak is more than 5 mA, so it trips.
Breaker protects wires. GFCI protects people.

ex.q: A device draws 8.000 A on the hot wire but only 7.992 A returns on neutral. Does a 5 mA GFCI trip?
steps: The leak is the missing current: 8.000 - 7.992.
Compare to the limit of about 5 mA.

ctrl-L2#2.trap: Thinking a GFCI is the same as a breaker. A breaker watches for a big current. A GFCI watches for a tiny mismatch. Both are needed.
ctrl-L2#2.tip: GFCI counts what goes out and what comes back.

ctrl-L3#0.why: A relay is an electromagnet with a switch. A small current in the coil makes a magnetic field. The field pulls a metal arm and closes (or opens) a separate contact. That second circuit can carry much more power, and it is electrically separate from the first. This lets a tiny signal, like a sensor or chip, control a motor or heater. When the coil is turned off, the collapsing field makes a voltage spike. A diode across the coil absorbs that spike.
ctrl-L3#0.pic: Draw a coil with a small battery and a button on the left. Draw a metal arm above the coil. On the right draw a motor circuit with a big battery and contacts that the arm closes. Put a diode across the coil, stripe toward the plus.
ctrl-L3#0.analogy: A relay is like a light touch on a big door button. A small push (coil current) opens a heavy door (big circuit). Small push = signal, door = load. It stops working because a door button stays pressed by you, while a relay holds itself only while current flows.
ways: Small coil current closes a switch for a big circuit.
12 V coil, 120 ohm: 0.1 A (1.2 W). It switches a 12 V, 10 A motor (120 W). 100 times the power.
Relay = remote-controlled switch. Diode across the coil.

ex.q: A relay coil is 12 V and 240 ohm. A 12 V, 5 A motor is switched by it. Find the coil current and the power ratio (motor to coil).
steps: Coil current: I = V / R = 12 / 240 = 0.05 A.
The motor takes 100 times more power than the coil.

ctrl-L3#0.trap: Forgetting the diode across the coil, or putting it backward. The spike when the coil turns off can destroy a transistor or chip. The diode must point so it blocks normal current.
ctrl-L3#0.tip: Relay: tiny trigger, big action, diode for the kick.

ctrl-L3#1.why: Current needs a complete path. In series, every switch is on the single path, so all must be closed: that is AND. In parallel, each switch gives its own path, so any one closed lets current through: that is OR. This links the wiring you can see with the logic you can write. The same idea scales up to lots of switches, and to logic gates in computers.
ctrl-L3#1.pic: Draw two switches in a line with a lamp and battery, and write AND beside it. Then draw two switches on separate branches with a lamp and battery, and write OR beside it. Mark the closed path in color for different switch settings.
ctrl-L3#1.analogy: A door with two locks needs both keys (AND, series). A building with two doors lets you in by either one (OR, parallel). Locks in a row = series, doors side by side = parallel. It stops working because keys are separate objects, while switches are connected by wire.
ways: Two switches, four settings. Series lamp ON: 1 of 4. Parallel lamp ON: 3 of 4.
AND: one line with two gaps. OR: two lines side by side, each with one gap.

ex.q: Switches A and B are wired in parallel to a lamp. For how many of the four on/off settings is the lamp on?
steps: Check A off, B off: no path, lamp off.
A on, B off: path through A, lamp on.
A off, B on: path through B, lamp on.
A on, B on: both paths, lamp on.

ctrl-L3#1.trap: Mixing up AND and OR. If you have to turn on all switches, it is series. If any one works, it is parallel. Draw it to check.
ctrl-L3#1.tip: Series: all aboard. Parallel: any one will do.

ctrl-L3#2.why: A three-way switch circuit lets you control one lamp from two places. Each switch is SPDT. The common of switch 1 connects to power, and the common of switch 2 connects to the lamp. Two traveler wires join the throws of the two switches. The lamp is on only when both switches connect to the same traveler. Flipping either switch moves to the other traveler, which breaks the path, and flipping the other restores it.
ctrl-L3#2.pic: Draw two SPDT switches side by side. Join the top contacts with one wire and the bottom contacts with another, and label them travelers. Connect the left common to the battery and the right common to the lamp. Trace the path in color for one setting.
ctrl-L3#2.analogy: Two light switches at both ends of a hallway. You flip one on the way in and the other on the way out. Switches = hallway ends, travelers = the two roads between them. It stops working because real hallway lights may be wired in more complicated ways in a house.
ways: Two SPDT switches, two travelers. Either flip changes the lamp.
Four settings: up-up ON, down-down ON, up-down OFF, down-up OFF. The lamp is on in 2 of 4.

ex.q: In a three-way circuit, both switches are set up and the lamp is on. You flip one switch. Then you flip the other. What are the lamp states?
steps: Start: both up, they connect to the same traveler, lamp ON.
Flip one: the switches now use different travelers.
No complete path, so the lamp is OFF.
Flip the other: both switches are down.
They connect to the same traveler again.
Answer: OFF after the first flip, ON after the second.

ctrl-L3#2.trap: Connecting the commons to the travelers. Travelers go from throw to throw. The commons go to power and to the lamp.
ctrl-L3#2.tip: Commons for power and lamp, travelers in between.

ctrl-L3#3.why: Switch circuits get confusing because the picture shows all switches at once. The fix is to freeze one setting, then redraw: a closed switch becomes a plain wire, and an open switch is simply removed. What remains is a small simple circuit that you can check by eye. Do this for each combination, or at least for the ones you care about. It turns a tricky puzzle into a series of easy ones.
ctrl-L3#3.pic: Draw the circuit once. Draw it again with each closed switch replaced by a straight line and each open switch erased. Circle whether the lamp still has a loop back to the battery.
ctrl-L3#3.analogy: It is like checking a maze: block off the doors that are closed and see if there is still a path from start to finish. Doors = switches, path = current. It stops working because a maze has just one entrance, but circuits can have several parallel paths.
ways: Redraw: closed switch = wire, open switch = gap.
S1 in series with (S2 parallel S3). Lamp on when S1 AND (S2 OR S3). That is 3 of 8 settings.
One redrawn picture per setting, each with a clear path or no path.

ex.q: S1 is in series with S2 and S3, which are in parallel with each other. How many of the 8 settings light the lamp?
steps: The logic is S1 AND (S2 OR S3).
S1 must be on, so only the 4 settings with S1 on matter.
Among them, S2 and S3 cannot both be off.
The settings (S2, S3) that work: on-on, on-off, off-on.
That is 3 settings, and off-off fails.

ctrl-L3#3.trap: Trying to solve it all in your head. Redraw for each setting. Count carefully so you do not skip a combination.
ctrl-L3#3.tip: Redraw it. Wire for closed, gap for open.

dcac-L1#0.why: DC means direct current: charge flows in one direction all the time. A battery has a fixed plus and minus, so it pushes one way. AC means alternating current: the push reverses again and again, so charge slides back and forth. The wall outlet in the US reverses 60 times each second (60 Hz). Lamps and heaters work with either, but many electronics need DC and use a charger to convert.
dcac-L1#0.pic: Draw a graph with time across and voltage up. For DC draw a flat horizontal line above zero. For AC draw a smooth wave that goes above and below the zero line. Mark one full wave as one cycle.
dcac-L1#0.analogy: DC is like a river that always flows downhill one way. AC is like ocean waves that push in and pull out at the shore. River = DC, waves = AC. It stops working because a wave moves water forward as well, but AC charge just wiggles back and forth in place.
ways: DC: one direction. AC: reverses direction again and again.
60 Hz AC makes 60 cycles per second. Each cycle has two reversals, so 120 direction changes per second.
DC is a flat line. AC is a wave crossing zero.

ex.q: US wall power is 60 Hz. How many times per second does the current change direction?
steps: 60 Hz means 60 full cycles each second.
One cycle goes forward, then backward.
So each cycle has 2 direction changes.

dcac-L1#0.trap: Thinking AC electrons travel all the way around the circuit. They mostly wiggle back and forth in place. Also, a battery is DC; do not say batteries make AC.
dcac-L1#0.tip: DC = Direct, one way. AC = Alternates, back and forth.

dcac-L1#1.why: The source decides the type. A battery or solar cell makes a steady voltage from a chemical or light effect, so it gives DC. A generator spins a coil in a magnetic field. As the coil turns, the field through it rises and falls and flips, so the voltage flips too, which gives AC. Power plants use big generators, so the grid carries AC. Chargers use diodes to turn that AC back into DC (rectifying) for phones and laptops.
dcac-L1#1.pic: Draw a coil spinning between a north pole and a south pole, with a meter next to it. Beside it draw the wave the meter would show. Next to that draw a battery and a flat line.
dcac-L1#1.analogy: A battery is like a water tower, always pushing one way. A generator is like a pedal on a bike: pushes in turns as the leg goes around. Tower = DC, pedal = AC. It stops working because a pedal has two legs pushing, but a generator coil makes the wave smoothly.
ways: Batteries and solar: DC. Generators and the grid: AC. Chargers rectify AC to DC.
12 solar cells at 0.5 V each in series make 6 V DC.
Chemical or light: DC. Spinning coil: AC.

ex.q: Twelve solar cells of 0.5 V each are connected in series. What is the voltage and is it AC or DC?
steps: Solar cells make a steady voltage from light.
A steady, one-direction voltage is DC.

dcac-L1#1.trap: Saying that anything plugged into the wall is AC at the device. Many chargers convert it to DC inside. The wall is AC, but your phone runs on DC.
dcac-L1#1.tip: Batteries stay put, generators go around.

dcac-L1#2.why: Power plants are often far from towns, so the wires are long and have some resistance. Heat lost in a wire is I^2 x R. Power delivered is V x I. For the same power, raising the voltage lowers the current. Cut the current to one tenth and the loss drops to one hundredth because of the square. Transformers raise and lower AC voltage easily, which is why the grid uses AC.
dcac-L1#2.pic: Draw a power plant on the left, a long thin wire in the middle, and a town on the right. Put a step-up transformer after the plant and a step-down transformer before the town. Mark the wire as high voltage, low current.
dcac-L1#2.analogy: Pushing a crowd through a hallway. One way is to send a few people very fast; the other is to send many people slowly. Fewer people means less bumping into walls. Bumping = heat loss, current = number of people. It stops working because people do not make heat by the square of their number.
ways: Higher voltage, lower current, less heat in the wires.
100 kW through 2 ohm wires. At 1000 V: 100 A, loss 20,000 W. At 10,000 V: 10 A, loss 200 W. 100 times less.
10 times the voltage means 1/100 of the loss.

ex.q: 100 kW is sent through wires of 2 ohm total. Compare the loss at 1000 V and at 10,000 V.
steps: Current is I = P / V, since P = V x I.
Answer: 20,000 W vs 200 W, 100 times less loss at 10,000 V.

dcac-L1#2.trap: Saying that high voltage itself wastes less because it is 'stronger'. The savings come from lower current, because loss is I^2 R.
dcac-L1#2.tip: Volts up, amps down, heat down.

dcac-L2#0.why: Each cell lifts charge by a fixed amount of voltage, like one step up a staircase. When you connect plus to minus, the charge climbs one step in the first cell and then another step in the next. The climbs add, so the voltages add. The same current flows through all the cells, so the battery's capacity stays the same as one cell. Four 1.5 V cells make 6 V. If you connect a cell backward, its step goes down and subtracts.
dcac-L2#0.pic: Draw cells as short and long lines (long = plus). Draw them in a row with plus of one touching minus of the next. Under each, write 1.5 V, then draw a bracket under all four with 6 V.
dcac-L2#0.analogy: Climbing stairs: each cell is a step 1.5 V tall, and stacking steps makes a higher staircase. Step = cell, height = voltage. It stops working because a staircase does not get tired, while the cell's capacity (current x time) does not rise in series.
ways: Series: plus to minus, voltages add, capacity does not.

ex.q: Four 1.5 V cells are in series, plus to minus. The last one is accidentally flipped. What is the total voltage?
steps: Three cells are correct: 3 x 1.5 = 4.5 V.
The flipped cell subtracts instead of adds.

dcac-L2#0.trap: Thinking that series adds capacity too. Voltage adds, but mAh stays the same as one cell. Also watch the orientation: a backward cell subtracts.
dcac-L2#0.tip: Series stacks the volts, like stairs.

dcac-L2#1.why: In parallel, plus joins plus and minus joins minus, so every cell sees the same voltage. Each cell can supply its own current, so the total available current and capacity add. That means the battery can run longer or push more current at the same voltage. Cells in parallel should be identical in voltage. If not, the stronger cell pushes current into the weaker one, which wastes energy.
dcac-L2#1.pic: Draw two cells side by side with plus wires connected along the top and minus wires along the bottom. Write 1.5 V next to the pair. Write 2000 mAh on each and 4000 mAh for the pair.
dcac-L2#1.analogy: Two water tanks feeding one pipe. The pressure is the same, but twice as much water is stored. Tanks = cells, pressure = voltage, water = capacity. It stops working because tanks of different heights would act like cells of different voltage, and that wastes energy.
ways: Two 1.5 V, 2000 mAh cells in parallel: 1.5 V, 4000 mAh. At 500 mA that lasts 4000 / 500 = 8 hours.
Parallel gives more time, not more volts.

ex.q: Three 1.5 V, 2500 mAh cells are in parallel and power a 500 mA load. How long do they last?
steps: The units: mAh divided by mA gives hours.

dcac-L2#1.trap: Adding the voltages in parallel. Voltage stays the same. What increases is the capacity and the amount of current available.
dcac-L2#1.tip: Parallel = parked side by side, longer ride.

dcac-L2#2.why: A cell needs two different metals in a liquid that has ions. One metal gives up electrons more easily than the other, so electrons collect on it. If you connect the two metals with a wire, those electrons flow through the wire to the other metal. The juice or salty water lets ions move inside so the charge can balance. The voltage depends on the metals, so copper with zinc gives more than copper with steel. A lemon cell is weak, about 0.7 V, so you need several in series.
dcac-L2#2.pic: Draw a lemon with two strips stuck in it, one copper and one steel or zinc, with a wire leading to a small meter. Label the strip that gives up electrons as minus. Draw an arrow from it through the wire to the other strip.
dcac-L2#2.analogy: Two kids on a seesaw of different weights: they do not balance, so one side goes down. Metals = kids, tendency to give electrons = weight. It stops working because a seesaw ends up balanced, but a cell keeps pushing until the chemicals are used up.
ways: Two different metals plus an ion-rich liquid make a cell.
Lemon 0.7 V each. Three lemons in series: 2.1 V, enough to light a red LED (about 1.8 V).
Different metals, juicy middle, voltage appears.

ex.q: Each lemon cell gives about 0.7 V. How many are needed in series to reach at least 2.0 V?
steps: Need N x 0.7 to be at least 2.0.
Round up to the next whole number: 3.

dcac-L2#2.trap: Thinking the lemon itself is the power source. The energy comes from the chemical reaction of the metals. The lemon only supplies the acid liquid for ions to move.
dcac-L2#2.tip: Two metals plus a wet middle make a cell.

dcac-L3#0.why: Period is the time for one full cycle of a repeating signal. Frequency is how many cycles fit in one second. They are opposites: a signal that repeats quickly has a short period, so T = 1 / f and f = 1 / T. A cycle that takes 0.1 s means 10 cycles fit in a second. Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), and one hertz is one cycle per second.
dcac-L3#0.pic: Draw a wave on a time axis. Mark where it begins to repeat and draw a double arrow across one cycle; label it T. Then count the number of cycles in a one second window and write f.
dcac-L3#0.analogy: A swing: the time for one back-and-forth is the period. The number of swings each minute is the frequency. Longer time for each swing means fewer swings. It stops working because a swing slows down, but a clean AC signal keeps the same frequency.
ways: Frequency = cycles per second. Period = seconds per cycle.

ex.q: A signal is 60 Hz. What is its period in milliseconds?

dcac-L3#0.trap: Forgetting the unit change. 0.1 s is 100 ms, not 0.1 ms. Always multiply seconds by 1000 to get milliseconds.
dcac-L3#0.tip: Frequency and period are flip partners.

dcac-L3#1.why: An AC voltage swings up and down, so its value is not constant. To compare it to DC, we ask: what DC voltage would make the same heat in a resistor? That is the RMS value (root mean square). For a smooth sine wave, the RMS is the peak divided by the square root of 2, about 0.707 of the peak. So the 120 V from a wall outlet is RMS, and the wave actually reaches about 170 V at the top.
dcac-L3#1.pic: Draw a sine wave with a horizontal dashed line at the top peak and another dashed line lower at about 70 percent of the peak. Label the top Vpeak and the lower line Vrms. Show that the wave spends only part of its time near the peak.
dcac-L3#1.analogy: A roller coaster: the highest point is the peak, but the average height of the ride is lower. The RMS is like an effective height. Peak = top of the hill, RMS = the useful level. It stops working because averages can cancel, but RMS is always positive.
ways: RMS is the DC-equivalent value. Peak = RMS x 1.414.
120 V RMS gives a peak of 169.7 V (about 170 V). 230 V RMS gives about 325 V peak.

ex.q: A European outlet is 230 V RMS. Find its peak voltage.
steps: The peak is higher than RMS for a sine wave.

dcac-L3#1.trap: Dividing when you should multiply. To go from peak to RMS you divide by 1.414. To go from RMS to peak you multiply. The peak must come out larger.
dcac-L3#1.tip: Peak is the proud tall one: RMS times 1.41.

dcac-L3#2.why: Harm comes from the current through the body, not directly from the voltage. By Ohm's law, I = V / R, so more voltage or less body resistance means more current. Wet skin has much lower resistance than dry skin, so the same outlet can push much more current. Around 10 to 20 mA can make muscles lock so you cannot let go. Larger currents can disturb the heartbeat. That is why you treat every outlet with respect.
dcac-L3#2.pic: Draw a stick figure touching a wire, with a path through the body to the ground. Label the current I, the body resistance R, and the voltage V. Draw two figures: one with dry hands (large R) and one with wet hands (small R).
dcac-L3#2.analogy: Water pressure through a hose: the pressure (voltage) matters, but the flow (current) is what knocks you over. A wider hose (wet skin, low resistance) lets more flow. Pressure = voltage, flow = current. It stops working because hoses do not stop heart muscles.
ways: Current does the harm. Wet skin allows more current.
120 V. Dry skin 100,000 ohm: 1.2 mA. Wet skin 1,000 ohm: 120 mA. (Example values only.)
Low resistance, more current, more danger.

ex.q: Using example values, find the current from 120 V through dry skin (100,000 ohm) and wet skin (1,000 ohm).
steps: Use Ohm's law: I = V / R.
Answer: 1.2 mA dry, 120 mA wet; the wet case is far above the 10-20 mA lock-up level.

dcac-L3#2.trap: Believing only high voltage is dangerous. Even household voltage can be deadly when your skin is wet. These are example resistances; real values vary a lot.
dcac-L3#2.tip: Wet hands, more amps: stay dry and stay safe.

dcac-L3#3.why: A normal AC outlet has three connections. The hot wire carries the alternating voltage from the panel. The neutral wire gives the current a path back to the panel. Under normal operation the load current goes out on hot and returns on neutral, so those two carry the same size current. The ground wire is a safety path, attached to the metal case, and normally carries nothing. If a hot wire touches the case, the fault current goes down the ground wire and trips the breaker instead of shocking you.
dcac-L3#3.pic: Draw a wall outlet with three slots. Label the short slot hot, the long slot neutral, and the round hole ground. Draw an appliance with a loop: arrow out on hot, arrow back on neutral, and a dotted line to the case on ground.
dcac-L3#3.analogy: A road trip with a safety road. Hot = the road out to the store, neutral = the road back home, ground = the emergency exit used only if something goes wrong. It stops working because exits are used rarely but are always connected.
ways: Hot: out. Neutral: back. Ground: safety only.
A 1200 W hair dryer on 120 V: 10 A on hot, 10 A back on neutral, 0 A on ground.
White = neutral, black = hot, green or bare = ground.

ex.q: A 1200 W hair dryer runs on 120 V. What current is in the hot, neutral and ground wires in normal use?
steps: The same current must return on neutral.
Ground only matters in a fault, so it carries 0 A.
Answer: hot 10 A, neutral 10 A, ground 0 A.

dcac-L3#3.trap: Calling the white wire ground. White is neutral and carries current back. Ground (green or bare) is only for safety. Both go to the panel but they do different jobs.
dcac-L3#3.tip: Hot goes, neutral returns, ground guards.

diode-L1#0.why: A diode has a built-in barrier at its junction that charges can cross only when pushed the right way. Push forward and the barrier drops, so current flows. Push backward and the barrier grows, so almost nothing flows. This one-way behavior comes from how the two silicon types meet, not from a moving part. Without it, a battery put in backward would push current the wrong way through a circuit and could damage it.
diode-L1#0.pic: Draw the diode symbol: a triangle pointing right with a bar at its tip. Draw an arrow along the triangle labeled current goes this way. Draw a curved arrow going the other way with an X on it.
diode-L1#0.analogy: A turnstile at a stadium that only turns one way. People are current, the turnstile is the diode. It stops working because a turnstile blocks everyone totally, while a diode passes a tiny leak and needs about 0.7 V of push to open.
ways: Triangle points the way current may go. The bar blocks the other way.
Silicon diode, 5 V forward: current flows, about 0.7 V across it. 5 V reverse: about 0 A.
Current goes with the arrow, not against it.

ex.q: A 9 V battery is hooked up backward to a motor. Where does a series diode go, and why does it save the motor?
steps: Place the diode in series with the motor, arrow pointing toward the motor.
Right way round: current flows with the arrow, motor runs.
Backward battery: the diode is reverse biased.
Reverse bias blocks current, so I is about 0.
No current means the motor sees nothing and is safe.

diode-L1#0.trap: Thinking the diode points the electron flow. The arrow points the way conventional current goes.
diode-L1#0.tip: Arrow says go; bar says no.

diode-L1#1.why: Pure silicon barely conducts. Doping adds a few foreign atoms. In N-type, extra electrons can roam. In P-type, missing electrons leave holes that act like moving plus charges. Join the two and electrons near the junction fall into holes. That leaves a thin zone with fixed charges, which makes the barrier. Forward bias means pushing electrons and holes toward that zone to shrink the barrier.
diode-L1#1.pic: Draw a rectangle split in half down the middle. Label the left P with small open circles for holes. Label the right N with small dots for electrons. Mark the middle line as the junction and put the plus battery terminal on P for forward bias.
diode-L1#1.analogy: A school dance with two rooms: one full of boys and one with empty chairs. Electrons are people, holes are empty chairs. The door between is the junction. It stops working because holes are not real particles, just missing electrons.
ways: P side: holes. N side: electrons. Forward means plus on P.
P at 1.0 V, N at 0.0 V: forward biased. P at 0.0 V, N at 1.0 V: reverse biased.
P-N: plus to P is Positive-Pass.

ex.q: The anode of a silicon diode is at 5 V. The cathode is at 4.3 V. Is it forward biased and does it conduct?
steps: Forward bias needs the P side (anode) higher than the N side (cathode).
Silicon needs about 0.7 V to open.
Yes, forward biased and it just conducts.

diode-L1#1.trap: Thinking P-type is positively charged. It is neutral overall. Holes are just spots missing an electron.

diode-L1#2.why: Doping works by changing how many outer electrons the atoms bring. Silicon has 4 outer electrons and makes 4 bonds. Boron has 3, so a bond is short one electron, which leaves a hole. Antimony has 5, so one electron is left over. Only a tiny amount is added, about one atom in millions, but it changes conduction a lot. Group number tells you the number of outer electrons.
diode-L1#2.pic: Draw a silicon atom as a dot with four lines to its neighbors. Replace one neighbor with a boron dot that has only three lines and a small open circle for a hole. Next to it draw an antimony dot with five lines, one line ending in an arrow for the free electron.
diode-L1#2.analogy: A row of 4-seat tables. Replace one table with a 3-seat table and one chair is empty (hole). Replace another with a 5-seat table and one person is standing (free electron). It stops working because the seats do not move, while holes drift around.
ways: Boron (Group 13) makes P. Antimony (Group 15) makes N.
Outer electrons: Si 4, B 3, Sb 5. Compare with 4: B is 1 short, Sb is 1 extra.
Less than 4: hole. More than 4: extra electron.

ex.q: Phosphorus is in Group 15. Added to silicon, what type is made and why?
steps: Silicon bonds use 4 electrons per atom.
Five minus four leaves one extra electron.

diode-L1#2.trap: Thinking N-type has a negative charge overall. It is neutral; each atom is balanced.
diode-L1#2.tip: Three is a hole, five is alive.

diode-L2#0.why: At the junction, electrons from the N side fall into holes from the P side. This leaves a thin strip with no free charges. The strip also has fixed charged atoms: negative on the P side, positive on the N side. Those fixed charges push back on any other charge trying to cross. So the strip is like a wall with a built-in voltage. About 0.7 V in silicon is the push needed to get over it.
diode-L2#0.pic: Draw the P and N blocks side by side. Between them, draw a narrow shaded strip labeled depletion region. Write minus signs on the P edge of the strip and plus signs on the N edge. Draw a tiny arrow across the strip pointing from N to P for the built-in push.
diode-L2#0.analogy: A moat around a castle. Charges are visitors, the moat is the strip. A forward voltage is a bridge that shrinks the gap. It stops working because a moat is stuck in place but this region grows and shrinks.
ways: Empty zone of fixed charges that blocks flow until pushed hard enough.
Forward bias: width shrinks. Reverse bias: width grows. 0 V applied: stays at its small default width.
Draw the zone narrow in forward, wide in reverse.

ex.q: A diode zone is thick. Is the diode forward or reverse biased, and does it conduct?
steps: A thick zone means a bigger wall.
A bigger wall happens under reverse bias.
Charges cannot cross a thick wall.
It is reverse biased and does not conduct.

diode-L2#0.trap: Saying the zone has lots of charges. It has none that are free to move.
diode-L2#0.tip: Forward: wall falls. Reverse: wall tall.

diode-L2#1.why: Forward bias connects plus to the P side. The battery pushes holes and electrons toward the junction. They fill the empty zone, so the wall gets thin. Once the push reaches about 0.7 V for silicon, charges cross and current rises very fast. The diode then holds near 0.7 V no matter how much current flows. Germanium needs only about 0.3 V because its barrier is smaller.
diode-L2#1.pic: Sketch a graph with voltage across the bottom and current up the side. Draw a flat line near zero, then a sharp turn upward at 0.7 V. Mark 0.3 V for germanium with a dotted line earlier on the same axis.
diode-L2#1.analogy: Pushing a heavy door that has a stiff latch. Below a certain push nothing moves. Once past the latch, it swings open easily. Push is voltage, latch is 0.7 V, door swinging is current. It breaks down because a door has no limit on current, but a diode burns if the current is too high.
ways: Plus on the anode shrinks the wall. Silicon opens at about 0.7 V.
Silicon: 0.3 V gives about 0 mA. 0.7 V gives a rising current.
Silicon about 0.7 V, germanium about 0.3 V, red LED about 1.8 V.

ex.q: A 5 V supply, a silicon diode, and a 430 ohm resistor are in series, forward biased. Find the current.
steps: Forward biased, so the diode drops about 0.7 V.
The resistor gets what is left: 5 - 0.7 = 4.3 V.
Current is 0.01 A, which is 10 mA.

diode-L2#1.trap: Treating a conducting diode as a plain wire with 0 V. It drops about 0.7 V.

diode-L2#2.why: Reverse bias puts plus on the N side. The battery pulls free electrons and holes away from the junction. The empty zone grows wider, so the wall gets taller. Almost nothing crosses, just a tiny leakage current. So the diode acts like an open switch, and the whole supply voltage ends up across it. That is why a backward LED stays dark.
diode-L2#2.pic: Draw P and N blocks with the depletion region in the middle drawn wide. Draw battery plus on the N side with arrows pulling away from the center. Label the leak as nearly zero.
diode-L2#2.analogy: A drawbridge that lifts when you push the wrong way: the more you push, the wider the gap. Voltage is the push, the gap is the zone. It stops working because a real bridge needs a motor, while this gap widens by itself.
ways: Reverse: wall grows, almost no current, acts open.
9 V battery, LED, 390 ohm, all backward: current is about 0 mA and the diode sees nearly 9 V.

ex.q: A 6 V battery is backward to a series LED and a 330 ohm resistor. What is the current and the LED voltage?
steps: The LED is reverse biased, so it is like an open switch.
An open switch passes about 0 current.
With zero current the resistor drops 0 V.
All 6 V is across the LED, and it stays dark.

diode-L2#2.trap: Thinking a backward LED blows right away. A small reverse voltage is fine; only large ones damage it.
diode-L2#2.tip: Back the wrong way, bright no way.

diode-L3#0.why: A normal diode is damaged when reverse voltage gets too large. A Zener is built to break down at a chosen voltage and survive it. In reverse breakdown, the voltage across it stays almost the same while the current changes a lot. That steady voltage is the point. A resistor in series limits the current so the Zener does not overheat.
diode-L3#0.pic: Draw the I-V graph again with the forward part on the right. On the left, draw the curve dropping sharply at a number like -5.1 V. Label that knee as the Zener voltage and note the line is almost vertical there.
diode-L3#0.analogy: A pressure relief valve on a water heater. Below the set pressure it stays closed. At the set pressure it opens and holds the pressure steady while water escapes. Pressure is voltage, escaping water is current. It stops working because a valve wastes water, but a Zener wastes power as heat.
ways: Zener runs backward on purpose to hold a set voltage.
A 5.1 V Zener on a 9 V source with a resistor: the load sees about 5.1 V.
Reverse side: flat near zero, then straight down at the Zener voltage.

ex.q: A 12 V supply feeds a 470 ohm resistor and a 5.1 V Zener in series. Find the Zener current.
steps: The Zener holds 5.1 V in reverse breakdown.
The resistor must drop the rest: 12 - 5.1 = 6.9 V.
Use I = V / R for the resistor.
Same series current goes through the Zener: about 14.7 mA.

diode-L3#0.trap: Hooking a Zener forward like a normal diode. It must be reverse biased to regulate.
diode-L3#0.tip: Zener zaps backward and stays steady.

diode-L3#1.why: An LED makes light when electrons drop into holes at the junction and give off the extra energy as a photon. The gap in energy depends on the material. A bigger gap gives a higher forward voltage and bluer light. Red has a smaller gap than blue. So red needs about 1.8 V and blue needs about 3 V. Because it is a diode, it only works one way, so the long lead (anode) goes toward plus.
diode-L3#1.pic: Draw the diode symbol with two small arrows pointing away from it, for light. Label the long lead + (anode) and the short lead - (cathode). Beside it write a small ladder: red 1.8, green 2.1, blue 3.0.
diode-L3#1.analogy: A ball falling from a table versus from a shelf: a taller drop gives more energy as a bounce. Gap size is drop height, light energy is bounce. It stops working because balls fall by gravity, while electrons are pushed by the supply.
ways: Bigger energy gap: higher voltage and bluer light.
Red 1.8 V, blue 3.0 V. On a 9 V supply the resistor drops 7.2 V with red but 6.0 V with blue.
Red is easy, blue is hard.

ex.q: A blue LED needs 3.0 V. What does a 5 V supply leave for the series resistor?
steps: The LED takes its forward voltage: 3.0 V.
Series drops add up to the supply, so this is right.

diode-L3#1.trap: Plugging the LED in backward and thinking it is broken. Check the long lead goes to plus.

diode-L3#2.why: Past about 1.8 V an LED current grows extremely fast with a tiny rise in voltage. Without a resistor, it would take too much current and burn out in a moment. The resistor takes up the extra voltage and sets the current. The resistor drops supply minus LED voltage, and Ohm's law gives its size. Rounding up lowers the current slightly, which is safe. Rounding down would push it past the target.
diode-L3#2.pic: Draw a loop: battery, resistor, LED. Write the supply voltage on the battery. Write V_LED beside the LED. Write the leftover next to the resistor with an arrow and the word drop.
diode-L3#2.analogy: A water slide with a long gentle ramp before the steep part. The ramp stops riders from reaching crazy speed. Ramp is the resistor, speed is current. It stops working because a ramp uses height, but a resistor uses voltage.
ways: Find the voltage the resistor must drop, then divide by the current you want.
9 V supply, red LED 1.8 V, 20 mA: R = 7.2 / 0.02 = 360 ohm. Next standard value up: 390 ohm.
Round up for safe, down for sorry.

ex.q: A 9 V supply powers a red LED (1.8 V) at 20 mA. Pick the standard resistor (330, 390, 470 ohm).
steps: 360 is not standard, so round up.
390 ohm gives 18.5 mA, below 20 mA, so safe.

diode-L3#2.trap: Rounding down. A smaller resistor gives more current than planned and may burn the LED.
diode-L3#2.tip: Up is safe, down is dumb.

diode-L4#0.why: LEDs in series share one current, so the same current goes through both. Their voltage drops add. In parallel, each LED has its own branch, but LEDs differ slightly. The one with a lower forward voltage hogs more current. Giving each branch its own resistor keeps the currents close. One shared resistor would let the stronger LED steal the current.
diode-L4#0.pic: Draw two loops from one battery: top loop LED with its own resistor, bottom loop the same. For series, draw one chain with both LEDs and one resistor. Put the same arrow I everywhere along it.
diode-L4#0.analogy: Two kids sharing one slide versus each having a slide of their own. Each has a line (resistor) so they go at the same speed. Slide is the LED, line is the resistor. It stops working because kids can be told to wait, but LEDs cannot.
ways: Series: add the drops. Parallel: one resistor each.
Two 2.0 V LEDs in series on 12 V at 20 mA: R = (12 - 4.0) / 0.02 = 400 ohm.
Series: one resistor total. Parallel: one resistor per branch.

ex.q: Two LEDs (2.0 V each) are in series on a 12 V supply at 20 mA. Find R.
steps: Series drops add: 2.0 + 2.0 = 4.0 V for the LEDs.
The resistor drops the rest: 12 - 4.0 = 8.0 V.

diode-L4#0.trap: Adding the LED currents in series. Current is shared there; only voltage adds.
diode-L4#0.tip: Series: voltage adds. Parallel: split resistors.

diode-L4#1.why: A diode that conducts in one direction can turn AC into DC. It passes the positive half and blocks the negative half. It protects against a reversed battery because the wrong polarity is blocked. Across a relay coil it gives the collapsing field's spike a path, so the spike cannot hurt a transistor. In a regulator, a Zener holds a set voltage. All uses come from the same one-way rule.
diode-L4#1.pic: Draw a sine wave. Draw the same wave below it with the negative humps flattened to zero. Label the first AC in and the second the half-wave rectified output.
diode-L4#1.analogy: A one-way street: traffic going the right way gets through, and traffic going the wrong way is turned back. Cars are current. It stops working because a street has no 0.7 V toll.
ways: One-way flow lets a diode rectify, protect, and regulate.
12 V in, silicon diode: the load sees about 12 - 0.7 = 11.3 V.
Input swings plus and minus. Output only has the plus half.

ex.q: A 12 V battery drives a 100 ohm load through a series silicon diode. Find the current.
steps: The forward diode drops about 0.7 V.

diode-L4#1.trap: Forgetting the 0.7 V drop. It matters most on low-voltage circuits.
diode-L4#1.tip: One lane: only the arrow gets through.

hands-L1#0.why: A breadboard has metal strips hidden under the holes. Each short column of five holes sits on one strip, so the five holes are the same wire. The center gap isolates the two halves so a chip can straddle it with each leg in its own column. The long rails run the whole length and are for power and ground. Knowing the hidden strips lets you wire without soldering.
hands-L1#0.pic: Draw a rectangle with rows of dots. Draw a thick line connecting the five dots in one short column. Draw a different thick line for the next column. Draw a gap in the middle with a chip bridging it. Draw two long lines along each edge labeled + and -.
hands-L1#0.analogy: A street with houses: each short column is a street where all five houses share the same road. The gap is a river between neighborhoods. Strip is the road, hole is a house. It stops working because a street is just a place, while a strip carries current.
ways: Five holes in a short column are one wire. The two halves of the board are separate.
Put a battery wire in column 10 and a resistor leg in column 10: they touch. A resistor in column 11 does not.
Short columns connect across, rails connect along.

ex.q: A resistor leg is in column 12 (left half). Where can the other part go to connect to it?
steps: Find the strip: column 12 on the left half.
All five holes in this column are connected.
Put the second part in one of the other four holes.
The right half would not touch it either.

hands-L1#0.trap: Plugging two parts into the same column and wanting them separate. They are wired together.

hands-L1#1.why: A multimeter has one dial for several jobs. The leads go in the right jacks so the current takes the path the meter expects. Black goes to COM, always. Red goes to V/Ohm for volts and ohms. The DC symbol is a straight line, the AC symbol is a wave. Starting on the highest range protects the meter from a value bigger than expected.
hands-L1#1.pic: Draw a round dial with positions: V with a straight line, V with a wave, ohm symbol, A. Draw two jacks under it: COM with a black wire and V/Ohm with a red wire. Mark an arrow on the top range.
hands-L1#1.analogy: Setting a radio before turning it up: dial the right band and keep the volume low. Dial is the function, range is the volume. It stops working because radios hide errors, but a wrong meter setting can blow a fuse.
ways: Red to V/Ohm, black to COM, straight line for DC, start on high range.
A 9 V battery on the 20 V range reads 9.00. On a 2 V range the meter would say overrange.
Straight for DC, wavy for AC.

ex.q: You want to measure a 9 V battery with ranges 2 V, 20 V, and 200 V. Which do you choose first and finally?
steps: Unknown size, so start high: 200 V.
Move down to 20 V for more digits.
The reading 9.04 now has better detail.
Final range: 20 V, because 2 V would overload.

hands-L1#1.trap: Leaving the red lead in the A jack when measuring volts. That jack is almost a short.

hands-L1#2.why: Voltage is a difference between two points, so the meter must touch both sides of the part. This is parallel. The meter has very high resistance, so it takes almost no current and does not change the circuit. If you put it in series instead, that high resistance would block nearly everything. The power must be on, because voltage only exists when the circuit is live.
hands-L1#2.pic: Draw a battery and a resistor in a loop. Add the voltmeter as a circle with V, with two wires bridging across the resistor like a bridge. Write power ON beside the battery.
hands-L1#2.analogy: Measuring the height of a hill by comparing top and bottom, not by walking through it. The two points are the probes. It stops working because a hill does not change when you measure it, but a poor meter can slightly change a circuit.
ways: Probes go across the part, in parallel, with power on.
9 V battery, 1 kilohm resistor, 2 kilohm resistor. Across 1 kilohm: 3 V. Across 2 kilohm: 6 V.

ex.q: A 12 V battery drives 100 and 300 ohms in series. What does a meter across the 300 ohm read?
steps: Place the meter across the 300 ohm part, in parallel.
